about: Causes: the cause→effect links the simulation models and the game teaches (learning-core design §3). Each chain step is backed by the cited docs/science section ('file.md#heading text'). 'pour' hints help find a new Wine that shows the Cause; 'line' is where it shows on a Tasting sheet. Topics paraphrase the Level 3 learning-outcome areas (no WSET wording). 'reviewBy': 'chain' marks Causes that practice pours rarely or never show (faults, sunburn, noble rot in the Mosel); they are reviewed with chain questions, and still tagged on the player's own Wines.

causes.title: A cool season keeps acidity high
chain: Cool nights and a cool season
slow the berry's respiration of malic acid
so the must keeps more malic acid and a lower pH
and the wine tastes high in acidity

causes.title: A warm season burns malic acid off
chain: A warm season and warm nights
speed up the berry's respiration of malic acid
so the must has less acid and a higher pH
and the wine tastes softer, lower in acidity

causes.title: Must weight sets the alcohol
chain: Riper grapes have more sugar (higher °Oe or °Brix)
yeast turn that sugar into alcohol
so a riper harvest gives a higher alcohol and fuller body
causes.topic: Grape growing: harvest timing and ripeness

causes.title: Ripeness moves the fruit character
chain: The later the grapes are picked
the further they ripen (more sugar, less acid and green character)
so the fruit moves from citrus and green fruit to stone and tropical fruit (whites), or from red to black fruit (reds)
causes.topic: Grape growing: harvest timing and ripeness

causes.title: Crop load sets concentration
chain: On an over-cropped vine (under about 0.8 m² of leaf per kg of fruit)
fewer bunches share the leaves' sugar among less fruit
so the grapes ripen further and the wine gains flavour intensity
causes.topic: Grape growing: yield and vine management
sources: canopy-and-yield.md#2.2 Leaf area to fruit ratio

causes.title: Spring frost kills young shoots
chain: A frost night after budburst
kills the young green shoots and their flower clusters
secondary buds replace only part of the crop
so yields fall, sometimes drastically

causes.title: Noble rot concentrates sweet wines
chain: Misty mornings then dry, sunny afternoons on ripe, intact grapes
let Botrytis grow without splitting the berries
the berries shrivel, concentrating sugar and acid and adding new aromas
so the wine shows honey, marmalade and dried apricot
causes.topic: Winemaking: sweet wines and sugar concentration

causes.title: Grey rot taints the wine
chain: Wet weather near harvest on damaged or tight bunches
lets Botrytis spread as grey rot
rotten fruit reaching the press brings mouldy, earthy off-flavours and oxidising enzymes
so the wine can be faulty and browner

causes.title: Shade and cool weather keep green pepper notes
chain: Bunches shaded before véraison, a cool season or an early harvest
keep more methoxypyrazines in the grapes
so the wine smells of green bell pepper and leaves
sources: canopy-and-yield.md#2.3 Fruit exposure and fruit-zone microclimate

causes.title: Sun on Riesling bunches builds the petrol note
chain: Bunches exposed to the sun (leaf removal, a sunny season)
build up carotenoid-derived TDN precursors
which turn into TDN as the wine ages in bottle
so older Riesling smells of petrol or kerosene
causes.topic: Grape growing: canopy management; wine ageing

causes.title: Riesling's floral terpenes
chain: Riesling grapes carry terpenes such as linalool
sun-exposed bunches make more of them
so the wine smells floral (blossom, citrus flower)
sources: canopy-and-yield.md#2.3 Fruit exposure and fruit-zone microclimate

causes.title: Sunburn gives cooked, bitter notes
chain: Bunches suddenly exposed to strong sun in a heatwave
overheat and burn
so the wine shows cooked fruit and bitter phenolics

causes.title: More extraction, more colour and tannin
chain: Warmer fermentation, more vigorous cap work and longer maceration
pull more colour and tannin out of the skins and seeds
so the red wine is deeper in colour and higher in tannin

causes.title: Unripe seeds give green, coarse tannin
chain: Grapes picked before the seeds turn brown
have green, astringent seed tannin
which extracts more in alcohol during long maceration
so the wine's tannin feels green and coarse
causes.topic: Grape growing: harvest timing; red winemaking

causes.title: Whole bunches add stem tannin and green, spicy notes
chain: Fermenting with whole bunches or added stems
brings stem tannin and stem aroma compounds (methoxypyrazines, eugenol) into the wine
so it gains tannin and, most from unripe stems, green, spicy, stalky notes

causes.title: A cool fermentation keeps fruity esters
chain: Fermenting white wine cool (about 14–16 °C)
makes the yeast form more fruity esters, and fewer escape with the CO₂
so the young wine smells of banana and pear drops

causes.title: Too little yeast nitrogen gives a rotten-egg smell
chain: A must low in yeast-assimilable nitrogen (below about 140–150 mg/L)
starves the yeast
which ferment slowly and release hydrogen sulphide (H₂S)
so the wine smells reduced (struck match, rotten egg)

causes.title: Stopping fermentation leaves sweetness
chain: Chilling the wine and adding SO₂ partway through fermentation
stops the yeast before all the sugar is used
so the wine keeps residual sugar and lower alcohol (a traditional Mosel method)

causes.title: Chaptalisation raises alcohol
chain: Adding sugar to the must before fermentation (where the law allows)
gives the yeast more sugar to convert
so the wine has more alcohol than the grapes alone would give

causes.title: Acidification freshens warm-climate musts
chain: Adding tartaric acid to the must (where the law allows)
raises titratable acidity and lowers pH
so a warm-climate wine tastes fresher and is more stable

causes.title: Malolactic conversion softens acidity
chain: Lactic bacteria convert sharp malic acid into softer lactic acid
titratable acidity falls and pH rises
so the wine tastes softer, rounder and less tart

causes.title: Malolactic conversion adds buttery notes
chain: Malolactic bacteria break down citric acid, making diacetyl as a by-product
so the wine can smell of butter and cream

causes.title: Lees ageing adds stability and subtle bread notes
chain: Ageing on fine lees, stirred now and then (bâtonnage)
dead yeast break down slowly (autolysis), releasing mannoproteins and savoury compounds
so the wine is more stable and can gain subtle bread or biscuit notes (strongest in sparkling wine)

causes.title: New French oak adds vanilla and toast
chain: New barrels still hold their oak compounds
vanillin and toasted-wood compounds (guaiacol, eugenol) move into the wine
so it smells of vanilla, toast, smoke and clove, and gains oak tannin

causes.title: Old barrels add little oak flavour
chain: Used barrels have given up most of their oak compounds
but still let a little oxygen through the wood
so the wine develops gently, with softer tannin in reds and little oak flavour

causes.title: Bottle age brings tertiary aromas
chain: Years in bottle
slowly transform primary fruit aromas and polymerise pigments and tannins
so the wine shows dried fruit, leather and forest floor, a garnet hue and softer tannins

causes.title: Age and high pH turn red wine garnet
chain: As a red wine ages, and more so at a higher pH
anthocyanins combine with tannins and lose their purple tone
so the colour moves from purple to ruby to garnet

causes.title: Too much oxygen oxidises the wine
chain: Oxygen exposure in the cellar or a poor seal
turns ethanol into acetaldehyde and browns the colour
so the wine smells nutty or of bruised apple and, beyond a limit, is faulty

causes.title: Brettanomyces gives barnyard notes
chain: High pH, little molecular SO₂ and used barrels
let Brettanomyces yeast grow after fermentation
making 4-ethylphenol
so the wine smells of leather, barnyard or sticking plaster

causes.title: Volatile acidity gives a vinegar lift
chain: Acetic acid bacteria or stressed yeast, helped by oxygen and low SO₂
make acetic acid
so the wine smells of nail varnish or vinegar; above the legal limit it is faulty

causes.title: SO₂ protects less at high pH
chain: Only the molecular form of free SO₂ protects the wine
its share falls steeply as pH rises
so high-pH wines need much more SO₂, or they risk spoilage (Brett, VA, oxidation)

causes.title: Skin contact releases tropical thiols
chain: Grape skins hold odourless thiol precursors
skin contact before pressing extracts more of them
and yeast release them as grapefruit and passion-fruit aromas

causes.title: Steep slopes mean hand labour
chain: A slope too steep for tractors
leaves every task, from pruning to picking, to hand labour, whatever the trellis
so a hectare needs two to five times the hours of tractor-worked land

causes.title: Lime starves sensitive rootstocks of iron
chain: Active lime in a marl or limestone soil
starves a lime-sensitive rootstock of iron (lime-induced chlorosis)
leaves yellow and photosynthesis falls
so the vine grows less, crops less and ripens less sugar
